name: Reading Comprehension
description: Authentic reading passages of 100 to 200 words on education, technology, travel, hobbies, health, environment, work, communication, science and culture, with main idea, detail, inference and vocabulary questions.

passages.title: A Library on Wheels
passages.content:
When Maria Kovalenko retired from teaching, her friends expected her to spend more time in her garden. Instead, she bought an old minibus, took out the seats and fitted it with shelves.

For the first month the bus stood outside her house while she painted it and sorted the books that neighbours had given her. Some of them were in poor condition, and she spent her evenings repairing covers with tape and glue. By the spring she had nearly nine hundred books, and she began to drive to three villages that no longer had a library of their own.

At first the visits were quiet. A few pensioners came to borrow detective stories, and children looked through the windows but did not come in. Maria soon realised that the children were not afraid of books; they were afraid of breaking something that looked so carefully arranged. So she put a box of old comics by the door with a sign that said 'Take one, bring one'. Within a week the box was empty, and the children were asking what else she had.

The bus now visits seven villages every fortnight. Maria no longer drives it alone: two of her former pupils share the driving, and a local shop pays for the fuel in exchange for a small advertisement on the side. Readers can order books by phone, and Maria writes their requests in a notebook that she keeps on the dashboard.

Asked why she did it, Maria says that she was never trying to save reading. 'People did not stop reading,' she explains. 'They stopped having a place to find the next book. The bus is just a way of bringing that place a little closer.'

passages.title: The Boy Who Fixed the Village Clock
passages.content:
For as long as anyone could remember, the clock on the old school building in Hartley had shown twenty past four. Visitors found it charming, (1) ______. So when fifteen-year-old Tom Price climbed a ladder with a toolbox one Saturday morning, most people assumed he would soon give up.

Tom had become interested in clocks after finding a broken alarm clock in his grandfather's shed. He took it apart, (2) ______, and put it back together until it worked. After that he read everything he could find about old mechanisms and watched hours of videos (3) ______.

The school clock was a far bigger challenge. Several parts had rusted, and one gear was missing completely. Tom made a careful drawing of it and asked a local engineering company (4) ______. The company agreed and even refused to take any money for the work.

It took him almost three months of weekends. On the day the clock finally started, a small crowd gathered in the square, and the head teacher (5) ______.

Tom now has a waiting list of neighbours with broken clocks. He says he enjoys the work because every mechanism is a puzzle, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Girl Who Mapped Her Town's Trees
passages.content:
When fourteen-year-old Solomiia Bondar noticed that several old chestnut trees on her street had been cut down, she wanted to know how many trees her town actually had. Nobody could tell her. The council kept records only of the trees in the central park, and even those were ten years out of date.

So Solomiia decided to count them herself. Every weekend for a whole summer she walked round a different district with a notebook, a tape measure and her phone. For each tree she recorded the species, measured the trunk and took a photo, then marked it on a free online map. At first her friends joked that she was spending her holidays talking to trees. By August, however, three of them had joined her, and a local teacher had shown them how to recognise diseased branches.

The map grew to more than four thousand trees. It showed something nobody had expected: the newer districts had almost no trees at all, while the old centre had lost a quarter of its chestnuts in ten years. When Solomiia presented the map at a council meeting, the adults in the room were silent for a moment. Then the head of the environment department asked whether they could use it.

Today the map is updated by volunteers from four schools, and the council checks it before approving any building work. Last spring the town planted six hundred young trees, most of them in the districts the map had shown to be bare. Solomiia, now at university, still gets messages from people who have spotted a tree that is not on the map. 'I did not set out to change anything,' she says. 'I just wanted an answer to a simple question.'

passages.title: The Orchestra from the Landfill
passages.content:
Cateura, a community on the edge of Paraguay's capital, Asunción, lies next to a huge landfill site. Many families there make a living by collecting and selling things that other people have thrown away. In the mid-2000s, an environmental worker called Favio Chávez came to the area to help with a recycling project. He was also a musician, and he began teaching music to a few local children.

There was a problem. A new violin cost more than many families earned in months, and there were never enough instruments to go round. So Chávez asked Nicolás Gómez, a local rubbish collector with a talent for building things, whether he could make instruments out of what the landfill offered. Gómez turned an old oil drum into a cello and made violins from tins and wooden boxes, using old forks and spoons for some of the parts.

The sound surprised everyone, including the children. The group became known as the Recycled Orchestra, and a film about them carried their story around the world. Since then the orchestra has performed in many countries and has shared the stage with well-known musicians.

For the young players, however, the most important change was not the travel. Several of them have gone on to study music, and some now teach younger children in Cateura. As Chávez once put it, the world sends them rubbish, and they send back music.

passages.title: The Stranger on the Night Train
passages.content:
Olha had taken the night train from Lviv to Kharkiv many times, but she had never shared her compartment with anyone (1) ______. The man in the seat opposite was about seventy and was studying a map so old that its edges had turned brown.

When the train stopped in the middle of a field for over an hour, he folded the map (2) ______. He told her that he had been born in a village near the railway line, a village that no longer existed. As a boy, he had watched the trains pass (3) ______.

Olha asked him why he had never come back before. He explained that he had spent most of his life abroad (4) ______. Now, after the death of his wife, he had finally decided to find the place where his house had stood.

At dawn the train slowed down near a row of old poplars. The man pressed his face to the window (5) ______. 'There,' he whispered, pointing at an empty field. Olha saw nothing but grass, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Night Shift at the Bakery
passages.content:
Every night at half past eleven, while the rest of the town is asleep, Andriy Kovach unlocks the back door of a small bakery on Shkilna Street. By four in the morning he has shaped six hundred rolls by hand. He has done this for nineteen years and says he has never once needed an alarm clock.

What is unusual about the bakery is not the bread but the two chairs by the oven. Three years ago a sixteen-year-old called Taras began stopping at the window on his way home. He was failing his exams, had no money and, as he later admitted, nowhere in particular to be. Andriy gave him a roll, and because the boy stayed until dawn, a job for the summer.

Word travelled. Four teenagers now work in the bakery in turns, two nights a week each, and none of them is paid in cash. Instead Andriy covers their textbooks, their bus passes and, in one case, a driving course. "Money disappears in a week," he says. "A driving licence does not."

The arrangement has its critics. A neighbour once complained to the labour inspectors, who arrived at two in the morning and found three sleepy students weighing flour. Nothing came of the complaint, but Andriy now writes down every hour anybody works.

He has been asked more than once to open a second bakery in the new district. He always says no. "I can teach four people properly," he says. "I cannot teach forty."

passages.title: The Man Who Mends Umbrellas
passages.content:
There is a workshop the size of a wardrobe under the stairs of a shopping centre in Lviv, and for eleven years it has belonged to Bohdan Prokopiv. He mends umbrellas. Nothing else. On a wet October day thirty people may queue outside it; in July he sometimes sees nobody at all.

Bohdan did not plan any of this. He worked as an engineer at a factory that closed in 2012, and for two years afterwards he repaired things for neighbours because it was the only work he could find. The umbrellas came last, and they stayed, because nobody else in the city would touch them. A new umbrella costs less than an hour of a mechanic's time, so shops simply advise customers to buy another one.

That advice is exactly what he argues against. He keeps a box of ribs, springs and handles taken from umbrellas beyond saving, and most repairs take him four minutes. He charges little and refuses tips. What he asks instead is that the customer stays and watches, so that next time the frame bends they might straighten it themselves.

His daughter has built him a website, which he has never looked at. Journalists call him the last umbrella master in Ukraine, a description he finds ridiculous. "There were four of us when I started," he says. "Three retired. That is not history. That is arithmetic."

passages.title: The School That Sails
passages.content:
The Amazon town of Belém has more water than road, and for years that arithmetic decided who went to secondary school. Children from the river communities could reach a classroom only by boat, and a boat cost money their families did not have. In 2016 a teacher named Ana Ribeiro suggested moving the classroom instead.

The result is a converted ferry with four rooms, a laboratory and a roof of solar panels. It leaves the port on Monday morning, stops at seven landing stages, and each stop has a timetable pinned to a post. Pupils board, study for two days and are put ashore where they live. Nobody travels for more than twenty minutes.

The idea was not welcomed at first. The regional authority argued that a floating school would be impossible to inspect and dangerous in the rainy season, when the current is strong. Ana's answer was to invite the inspectors aboard for a full week. They came, they marked the exercise books, and the licence was granted three months later.

Today the ferry carries about two hundred pupils and has a waiting list. What surprises visitors is not the lessons, which look like lessons anywhere, but the silence at four o'clock, when the engine starts and thirty teenagers sit on the deck doing homework because there is nothing else to do until the next landing stage.

passages.title: Forty Years of Counting Birds
passages.content:
On the first Sunday of every month since 1984, Halyna Shevchuk has walked the same six kilometres along the Desna and written down every bird she has seen. The route has not changed. Neither has the notebook: she is on her forty-first, and they are stacked in a cupboard in the order they were filled.

For most of those years nobody asked to see them. Halyna was a chemistry teacher, not a scientist, and she began counting simply because a colleague had lent her a field guide and she wanted to use it. She sent her totals once to a research institute in the 1990s and received no reply.

That changed in 2019, when a doctoral student looking for long records of river birds found a mention of her in a local newspaper. Her notebooks turned out to contain something no funded project had: an unbroken monthly series covering thirty-five years, taken by one observer, in one place, using one method. Two of the species she recorded in the 1980s have not been seen on the Desna since 2004.

Halyna is now named on four scientific papers, which amuses her more than it pleases her. She has been careful to say in every interview that she is not a researcher and that the work required no talent whatsoever. "It required Sundays," she says. "Anybody has those."

passages.title: The Café Where Nothing Is Sold
passages.content:
On the last Saturday of the month the community hall in Chernivtsi fills with toasters. People carry in kettles, lamps, bicycles, a sewing machine, once an accordion, and sit down at long tables opposite a volunteer with a screwdriver. Coffee is free. So is the repair. Nothing in the room is for sale, which is why it is called a repair café rather than a workshop.

The rule that makes it work is that the owner stays at the table. Volunteers are not allowed to take an item away and hand it back mended; the owner holds the torch, passes the parts and, wherever possible, does the last step. About a third of the visitors come back the following month with something they have fixed alone.

Not everything can be saved. Modern kettles are glued rather than screwed together, and printers are designed so that opening them breaks them. The organisers keep a note of what defeats them and send the list once a year to two manufacturers, who have never replied.

The café now has imitators in six towns, and the organisers are asked constantly how to start one. Their answer disappoints people who expect equipment: find a hall, find four patient people and put up a poster. "The tools are the easy part," says one of them. "Patience is the rare tool."

passages.title: The Last Cinema in Town
passages.content:
When the cinema in Sokal closed in 2009, its projector stayed where it was, because moving it would have cost more than it was worth. The building became a furniture shop, then a gym, then nothing at all. In 2021 three former pupils of the town's school bought the lease with money they had saved abroad and opened the doors again, with the same projector and a great deal of dust.

They were told the plan made no sense. The nearest multiplex is forty minutes away, every household has a subscription service, and the town has fewer than nine thousand people. The three of them accepted all of this and built the programme around it. They show two films a week, both chosen by a vote on a noticeboard in the foyer, and they never show anything that is still in the multiplex.

The result has been busier than anyone predicted, although not in the way cinemas usually measure. Ticket sales cover about half the costs; the rest comes from the hall being used on weekday mornings by a choir, a chess club and a course in spoken English. The cinema is open forty hours a week and shows films for six of them.

Asked whether it is really a cinema, one of the owners shrugs. "It is a room with chairs and a dark wall," he says. "That was always the useful part."

passages.title: A Diary of Rain
passages.content:
Marko Ilchenko was eleven when his grandmother gave him a rain gauge, a plastic cylinder that cost almost nothing and that he fixed to a fence post in the garden. She told him to read it at eight every morning and write the number down. He did so for a week out of politeness and then, for reasons he still cannot explain, for the next nine years.

The diary is not interesting to read. Each line contains a date, a figure and, very occasionally, a word: hail, fog, nothing. What makes it unusual is that the village has no weather station, and the nearest official gauge is twenty-six kilometres away, on the other side of a range of hills that changes the rainfall completely.

In 2023 the village applied for money to rebuild a bridge that floods twice a year. The application required evidence that the flooding was getting worse, and the regional figures showed no such trend, because they were measured in a different valley. Marko's diary did. The bridge was rebuilt last spring.

He is now studying engineering and has handed the gauge to his cousin, with the same instruction his grandmother gave him. He admits he expected nothing to come of nine years of numbers. "It was not science," he says. "It was a habit. The science was an accident."

passages.title: Borrowing Seeds
passages.content:
A library card in the town of Nizhyn will get you a novel, a dictionary or two hundred grams of tomato seeds. The seed library occupies four drawers of an old card catalogue by the window, and it works on the same principle as the shelves behind it: take what you need, and bring back more than you took.

That last part is the difficulty. A borrowed book comes back unchanged; borrowed seeds come back only if somebody lets a plant go to seed instead of eating it, dries what it produces and remembers to return in October. In the first year the library lent nine hundred packets and received eleven back.

The librarians responded by teaching rather than complaining. They ran four evening classes on saving seed, put a note in every packet explaining which plants are easy to save from, and started lending only those varieties: beans, peas, tomatoes, lettuce. Cucumbers and carrots were quietly removed, because they cross with anything nearby and beginners are almost guaranteed to fail with them.

The return rate is now above forty per cent, and the drawers hold varieties that no shop in the region sells, including a small yellow tomato brought from a village in the Carpathians by a reader's grandmother. Its label says only "Hanna's, 1974". Nobody knows anything else about it, and it grows better here than anything bought in a packet.

passages.title: Letters to the Lighthouse
passages.content:
The lighthouse on the spit stopped working in 1998, when a satellite system made it unnecessary, and the last keeper left with his dog and a box of logbooks. The building was locked and forgotten for twenty years, until the regional museum agreed to open it on summer weekends and asked for a volunteer to sit at the door and sell tickets.

The volunteer was Oksana Tymko, then seventy-one, who had grown up in the nearest village and remembered the light from her childhood. She sold about nine tickets a day. Between visitors she began answering the letters that arrived at the lighthouse, which nobody had thought to redirect, and which were still coming: enquiries from ship enthusiasts, questions from schoolchildren, one every few months from a former sailor in Gdansk.

She answered all of them by hand, signing herself "the lighthouse". Within two years the letters had multiplied tenfold, and the museum, which had considered closing the site, found itself running a correspondence. Oksana now has three helpers and a rule she enforces strictly: no printed replies and no letter left longer than a fortnight.

The building is no more useful to shipping than it was in 1998. What the light does now, she says, is slower. "A ship saw it for a second," she says. "A letter is a lighthouse that arrives at your house and stays on the table."

passages.title: The Bench by the Bus Stop
passages.content:
The bus stop on the edge of Radomyshl had a timetable, a metal pole and nothing else, (1) ______. In winter that wait was long enough to be unpleasant, and the people who waited were mostly women coming back from the market with heavy bags.

In 2019 a carpenter called Yurii Panasiuk decided to build a bench there. He did not ask anybody, (2) ______. The bench appeared on a Tuesday morning, painted green, screwed into two concrete blocks he had carried out himself.

The council removed it eleven days later. An official explained on the telephone that anything standing on municipal land had to be approved, and that unapproved furniture (3) ______. Yurii listened, thanked her, and built a second bench.

That one lasted five weeks. The third lasted until the following spring, by which time the story had reached a regional newspaper and a photograph of the empty concrete blocks (4) ______. The council changed its position, though it did not say so directly. Instead it announced a small budget for seating at rural stops and invited applications.

Yurii's application was approved in June, and he now builds benches for eleven villages, (5) ______. He is paid for the materials but not for his time, which he says is the arrangement he would have chosen anyway.

The original green bench was never returned. Nobody knows where it went, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Woman Who Named the Streets
passages.content:
When the new district of Vyshneve was finished in 2017, it had four thousand flats and no street names. The builders had used letters — Block A, Block B — and for two years the post office simply guessed, (1) ______.

Liudmyla Harasym, who had moved there from a village of eighty people, found this unbearable. She began by asking her neighbours what they would call the streets, (2) ______. Most of them shrugged. A few suggested the names of poets, which she wrote down without enthusiasm, because every second district in the country already had them.

Then she changed the question. Instead of asking what the streets should be called, she asked what had stood there before the district was built. That question people could answer. There had been an orchard, a brick works, a path that flooded every March and a well (3) ______. Within a month she had nineteen pages of notes.

The proposal she sent to the council contained eleven names, none of them commemorating a person. The council, which had expected the usual list, (4) ______ and asked her to present it in public. Two hundred people came, which is more than had come to any meeting about the district before.

Nine of the eleven names were adopted. Liudmyla, who is now sixty-eight, says the argument that convinced the room was not historical at all. A name taken from the place, she told them, is the only kind (5) ______, because it does not have to be explained to a child, (6) ______.

passages.title: A Letter That Took Sixty Years
passages.content:
In March 2022 a builder replacing the floor of a post office in Drohobych found a canvas sack under the boards. Inside were forty-one letters, all postmarked between 1958 and 1961, (1) ______. Nobody has ever established how they got there.

The regional postal service decided to deliver them. This sounded simpler than it was: of the forty-one addresses, nineteen no longer existed, (2) ______. A retired sorter named Ivan Dutko volunteered to trace what he could, and spent fourteen months doing it.

He delivered eleven letters to the people they had been written to. Six of those eleven were read in front of him, (3) ______, and he has refused ever since to describe what was in them. Another nine went to children or grandchildren of the addressee. The rest were placed in the regional archive, where anybody who can prove a connection (4) ______.

What surprised Ivan was how little the letters contained. Almost all of them were ordinary: a cousin asking about a job, a soldier describing the food, a woman explaining (5) ______. He had expected, he admits, something more dramatic.

He was asked afterwards whether the delivery had been worth fourteen months of his time. He said that the question assumed the letters were the point, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Orchard Nobody Owned
passages.content:
Between the railway and the allotments on the eastern side of Nizhyn there are ninety-three fruit trees, (1) ______. They were planted in the 1970s by the railway, which wanted a windbreak, and forgotten when the line was electrified.

For thirty years local people picked the fruit quietly and said nothing, on the reasonable assumption that asking a question (2) ______. Then in 2018 a fence appeared along one edge, and a rumour went round that the land had been sold.

It had not. A student called Nazar Bondarenko spent a winter in the land registry and established that the strip belonged to nobody at all: the railway had given it up in 1996, (3) ______. Legally it was what lawyers call abandoned, which in Ukraine means it reverts to the community.

The community, however, had to notice. Nazar printed the registry extract, pinned it to the fence, (4) ______. Forty-six people came to the first meeting, mostly to argue. By the third meeting they had agreed a rota for pruning, a rule that anybody may pick what they can eat that day, (5) ______.

The orchard is now formally registered to the town and informally run by eleven households. The fence came down in 2021. Nazar, who has since moved to Kyiv, says the legal part took four months and the human part (6) ______.

passages.title: The Map Made of Footsteps
passages.content:
The official map of the park in Bila Tserkva showed eleven paths. The park actually had nineteen, (1) ______ — the shortcuts people had worn across the grass over forty years of walking to the station.

In most towns those paths are dealt with by putting up a sign or a low fence. The new park manager, Olena Kravets, did the opposite. In her first spring she photographed the park from above once a fortnight, (2) ______, and by September she had a picture of exactly where people walked.

Then she paved them. Not all of them: two crossed ground that floods, and one ran through the only patch of the park where a rare orchid grows, (3) ______. The other five were laid in gravel over the winter, following the lines in her photographs to within half a metre.

The reaction was not what she expected. Several residents complained that paving the shortcuts (4) ______, and a letter to the newspaper accused her of rewarding laziness. Olena's answer was that the paths had existed for four decades, (5) ______, and that all she had done was stop pretending otherwise.

Three years later the grass between the paths has recovered completely, which was the part nobody predicted. When a route is comfortable, she says, people stay on it, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Choir That Meets on the Platform
passages.content:
Platform 2 of Konotop station is used by four trains a day. Between them it is empty for hours, (1) ______, and in 2016 a music teacher named Vira Ostapchuk asked the station master whether she could use it.

He assumed she wanted to give a concert. What she wanted was somewhere to rehearse. The school hall was booked every evening, the church would not take a choir that sang anything other than hymns, and the platform had a roof, a wall of tiles (2) ______ and, crucially, nobody to disturb.

Permission was given for a month. The choir is still there eight years later. It rehearses on Wednesdays from six until half past seven, stopping twice for the trains, (3) ______. Passengers waiting on the platform are neither invited to join in nor asked to move.

A few things have changed. The choir now has thirty-one members, up from nine, and the station has installed two benches (4) ______. Twice a year it sings at weddings, which is where its money comes from. It has never once performed a concert on the platform itself, (5) ______.

Vira was asked recently what she would do if the station closed. She said she had thought about it a great deal and had concluded that a choir needs three things: a roof, an hour, and a place (6) ______.

passages.title: The Postman Who Learned to Sign
passages.content:
Serhii Marchuk delivered letters in the same three streets for nineteen years. On one of them lived a deaf couple, the Kozaks, and for the first eleven of those years his entire communication with them (1) ______.

He began learning sign language in 2014, at forty-six, for a reason he describes as embarrassing: a parcel needed a signature, he could not explain which box it was in, and the exchange lasted, by his own estimate, (2) ______. He went home and looked up an evening course the same night.

Learning it took him three years and he was, he says, the worst student in the class. What kept him going was that the course was full of people (3) ______ — a nurse, two teachers, a woman whose grandson had been born deaf — and none of them found it easy either.

The Kozaks noticed the first time he signed a complete sentence. Mrs Kozak told a local reporter, years later, that she had assumed he was ill, (4) ______.

Serhii retired in 2021 and now teaches a short course at the postal training centre, (5) ______. He is careful about how he describes it. He did not learn a language to help anybody, he says. He learned it because standing on a doorstep unable to say anything (6) ______.

passages.title: The Shop With No Prices
passages.content:
The vegetable shop that Olha Verbytska runs in a small town near Poltava has no price labels on anything, (1) ______. Customers fill a bag, put it on the scales and are told a figure that Olha works out in her head.

This is not a philosophy. It began because the shop opened in a week when prices were changing daily and she could not keep up with the labels, (2) ______. By the time prices settled she had discovered something she had not expected: without labels, people asked her questions.

They asked what was cheap that week, what had come from nearby, what was worth buying in quantity, (3) ______. Almost nobody had asked her anything in the seven years she had worked behind a till in a supermarket.

She now sets her prices every morning, and she does adjust them for people she knows are struggling, (4) ______. When a journalist asked her about this directly, she refused to discuss individual customers and said only that the scales tell the truth and the rest is her business.

The arrangement makes some visitors uncomfortable. A few walk out, (5) ______. Olha does not try to stop them. She says a shop without labels asks for a kind of trust that cannot be requested, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Class That Wrote a Dictionary
passages.content:
A teacher in a village school in the Zakarpattia region gave her fourteen-year-olds an assignment in 2019: write down every word your grandparents use (1) ______. She expected perhaps forty words and a short discussion about dialect.

The class brought back six hundred and twelve. Some were old agricultural terms, some were borrowings from Hungarian or Slovak, and a surprising number were words for weather (2) ______. Several pupils reported arguments at home about whether a word was "real", (3) ______.

The teacher, Nataliia Fedak, did not know what to do with the list, so she did the obvious thing and turned it into the next term's work. Pupils checked each word with a second speaker, recorded a sentence containing it, (4) ______, and marked the ones nobody under sixty used any more. That last column turned out to be four hundred words long.

A university in Uzhhorod heard about the list in 2021 and offered to publish it. Nataliia agreed on one condition: that every pupil (5) ______. The book appeared in 2023 with thirty-one names on the cover under hers.

She is asked fairly often whether the project was about saving the dialect. She says it was not, (6) ______.

passages.title: The Lamp in the Window
passages.content:
The house at the end of Sadova Street has had a lamp burning in its upstairs window every night since 1994, (1) ______. For the first fifteen years nobody in the street knew why, and the family who lived there did not volunteer an explanation.

The lamp was lit by Mariia Onyshchenko for her son, who left for seasonal work in 1993 and did not come back. She was told in 1996 that he had almost certainly died, (2) ______. She lit the lamp anyway, every evening at dusk, for twenty-two years.

What makes the story unusual is what happened after her death in 2016. Her neighbour, a man in his thirties who had never spoken to her at length, (3) ______. He did it for a week, he says, because switching it off felt like a decision that was not his to make.

The week became a year. In 2018 two other households on the street began lighting lamps of their own, (4) ______, and by 2021 there were nine. Nobody organised this and there is no association, no fund and no annual event.

Journalists have come to the street three times and each time have gone away slightly disappointed, (5) ______. The neighbour says that is exactly right. It is not a memorial, he says, and it is not a message. It is a lamp somebody used to light (6) ______.

Read the text and answer the question.

The school library at Brookfield was almost closed three years ago. Fewer than twenty pupils used it each week, and the governors argued that the space would be better used as an extra classroom. Instead, a new librarian persuaded them to give her one term to change things. She moved the shelves away from the walls to create small reading corners, ordered graphic novels alongside the classics, and opened the room at lunchtime for a book club that pupils themselves ran. Borrowing rose slowly at first, then sharply. By the end of the year, more than two hundred pupils were using the library every week, and teachers reported that reluctant readers were finishing whole books for the first time. The governors quietly abandoned the plan to convert the room. What had seemed to be a problem of space, the librarian later said, had really been a problem of welcome.

What was the governors' original plan for the library?
options: To turn the room into an extra classroom.
To move the library to a larger building.
To replace the librarian with a volunteer.
To open the room only at lunchtime.

Ovens are never the same temperature.

For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as an empty space between periods of useful activity, and shortening it was widely admired. Research over the past three decades has reversed that view completely. During sleep the brain does not switch off; it consolidates what was learnt during the day, clears waste products that accumulate in waking hours and regulates the hormones that govern appetite and stress. As a medical condition requiring treatment.
As the most important part of the day.
As a habit that varied with the seasons.

City councils across Europe have begun planting trees at a rate not seen for a generation, and the reasoning has shifted. Trees were once planted chiefly because they were pleasant to look at. They are now planted as infrastructure. A mature street tree cools the air around it by several degrees on a hot day, intercepts rainfall that would otherwise overwhelm the drains, and traps a measurable quantity of the fine particles produced by traffic. None of these benefits arrives quickly. A sapling delivers almost nothing in its first decade, which is precisely why planting programmes are vulnerable: the councillors who pay for them will not be in office when the trees begin to work. Cities that have succeeded tend to be those that made maintenance, rather than planting, the measure of success. Counting the trees still alive after ten years turns out to be a far more demanding target than counting the ones put into the ground.

Councils now plant trees to replace drains.
Trees are chosen for their appearance in winter.

Ice cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet are among the most informative objects in climate science, and their value depends on a simple physical accident. As snow accumulates and is compressed into ice, it traps tiny bubbles of the air that surrounded it. Those bubbles are not a proxy or an estimate; they are samples of the actual atmosphere of the year in which the snow fell. A core several kilometres long therefore contains a sequential archive stretching back hundreds of thousands of years, from which the composition of past atmospheres can be measured directly. The chief difficulty is not extraction but dating. Layers near the surface are distinct and can be counted like tree rings, but under the pressure of the ice above them the deeper layers thin and deform until individual years become indistinguishable, and researchers must turn to indirect methods whose margins of error widen with depth.

What makes the bubbles in an ice core so valuable?
options: They are actual samples of the atmosphere of the year the snow fell.
They indicate how much snow fell in a given year.
They reveal the temperature at the surface of the ice.
They contain traces of ancient plant material.
questions.explanation: Бульбашки цінні тим, що це справжні зразки атмосфери того року, коли випав сніг.

Few debates in the museum world are as difficult as the question of restitution. Many of the objects in European collections arrived during periods of colonial rule, under conditions that would not be accepted today, and the countries they came from have asked for them back. The arguments against returning them have grown weaker over time. Claims that receiving institutions lack the facilities to care for objects have been answered by the construction of well-equipped museums in the countries concerned, and the fear that one return would empty every gallery in Europe has not been borne out where returns have taken place. What remains genuinely hard is the detail. Ownership records are often incomplete, several parties may have a legitimate claim to the same object, and legislation in some countries actively prevents national collections from giving anything away. Progress, where it has been made, has usually come from long negotiation rather than from any single decision of principle.

What has weakened the argument about receiving institutions?
options: Well-equipped museums have been built in the countries making claims.
Fewer objects are now requested than in the past.
European museums have run out of storage space.
International law now requires immediate return.

while his wife slept in the next carriage
questions.explanation: Після anyone у (1) потрібне порівняння з цим попутником; після folded the map у (2) — наступна дія; у (3) продовжується спогад про потяги; у (4) — пояснення, чому він не повертався; у (5) — як він дивився у вікно; у (6) yet протиставляє порожнє поле кивку Ольги. Фрагмент про розпродані квитки не пасує ні до чого, а про дружину в сусідньому вагоні суперечить тексту: дружина померла.

questions.title: What is unusual about Andriy's bakery, according to PARAGRAPH 2?
options: the people who work there
the hour the bread is baked
the recipe for the rolls
the place it is built in
questions.explanation: Незвичайні не хліб і не години, а двоє крісел біля печі — тобто підлітки, які там працюють.

questions.title: How does Andriy pay the teenagers who work for him?
options: in things, not in money
in cash at the end of the week
in bread and a hot meal
with a share of the profits
questions.explanation: Готівки він не дає: оплачує підручники, проїзд, курси водіння.

questions.title: Why did the labour inspectors come to the bakery?
options: a neighbour complained
a student had been injured
Andriy had invited them
the oven was found unsafe
questions.explanation: Перевірку викликала скарга сусіда, а не пригода чи прохання.

questions.title: What changed in the bakery after the inspection?
options: Andriy records every hour
the teenagers left
the bakery closed at night
Andriy hired an adult
questions.explanation: Справу закрили, але відтоді Андрій записує кожну відпрацьовану годину.

questions.title: Why does Andriy refuse to open a second bakery?
options: he could teach only four
the rent there is too high
he is close to retirement
nobody would buy the bread
questions.explanation: Причина в навчанні: «Я можу навчити чотирьох як слід, а сорока — ні».

questions.title: What do we learn about Bohdan's workshop in PARAGRAPH 1?
options: weather decides its trade
it has moved several times
it is open only in autumn
it employs thirty people
questions.explanation: У дощ — черга з тридцяти, у липні — нікого: робота залежить від погоди.

questions.title: Why did Bohdan start repairing things?
options: his factory had closed down
he had always enjoyed it
his neighbours asked him to
he wanted to leave engineering
questions.explanation: Завод закрився 2012 року, і ремонт був єдиною роботою, яку він знайшов.

questions.title: Why do shops tell customers to buy a new umbrella?
options: a repair costs more
the old ones are unsafe
they have no spare parts
the frames cannot be bent
questions.explanation: Нова парасолька коштує менше, ніж година роботи майстра.

questions.title: What does Bohdan ask of his customers?
options: to watch how he does it
to pay whatever they can
to bring the broken ribs
to come back in a month
questions.explanation: Замість чайових він просить подивитися на ремонт, щоб наступного разу впоралися самі.

questions.title: How does Bohdan react to being called the last umbrella master?
options: he thinks it is nonsense
he is quietly proud of it
he uses it in advertising
he refuses to discuss it
questions.explanation: Він вважає це смішним: троє колег просто пішли на пенсію, це арифметика, а не історія.

questions.title: What problem does PARAGRAPH 1 describe?
options: the boat cost money
the schools were too small
the river was often closed
few teachers lived nearby
questions.explanation: До школи можна було дістатися лише човном, а човен коштував грошей.

questions.title: How does the floating school work?
options: it stops at seven villages
it stays at one landing stage
it sails in the dry season only
it teaches pupils at home
questions.explanation: Пором іде за розкладом, зупиняється на семи причалах і висаджує учнів там, де вони живуть.

questions.title: Why did the authority object to the project?
options: inspection would be hard
the ferry was far too old
the parents had not agreed
it would cost far too much
questions.explanation: Казали, що плавучу школу неможливо перевірити й небезпечно водити в сезон дощів.

questions.title: How did Ana answer the objection?
options: she invited them aboard
she changed the timetable
she wrote to the newspapers
she bought a second ferry
questions.explanation: Вона запросила інспекторів на цілий тиждень, і ліцензію дали.

questions.title: What surprises visitors to the ferry?
options: what pupils do on deck
the size of the classrooms
the noise during lessons
the age of the teachers
questions.explanation: Дивує не урок, а тиша о четвертій, коли тридцятеро підлітків роблять уроки на палубі.

questions.title: What has stayed the same since 1984?
options: the route Halyna walks
the number of birds
the notebook she writes in
the people who join her
questions.explanation: Маршрут не змінювався; зошит уже сорок перший, а птахів меншає.

questions.title: Why did Halyna begin counting birds?
options: she wanted to use a book
a school project asked her to
an institute had hired her
she was training as a scientist
questions.explanation: Колега позичив їй визначник, і вона захотіла ним скористатися.

questions.title: What happened when she first sent her totals to an institute?
options: nobody answered her
her figures were corrected
she was invited to work there
the data were published
questions.explanation: У 1990-х відповіді вона не отримала; увагу звернули аж 2019 року.

questions.title: What made the notebooks valuable to researchers?
options: one person kept them going
they described rare species
they covered the whole country
they were written by a teacher
questions.explanation: Цінність — у безперервному ряді: один спостерігач, одне місце, один метод.

questions.title: How does Halyna describe her own work?
options: as a matter of free time
as the result of training
as a lifelong ambition
as a duty to her town
questions.explanation: «Це потребувало неділь. Вони є в кожного» — жодного таланту, лише час.

questions.title: Why is the place called a café rather than a workshop?
options: nothing there is sold
it also serves meals
it opens in the evening
it is run by one family
questions.explanation: Ремонт і кава безкоштовні, у залі нічого не продають — звідси й назва.

questions.title: What must the owner of a broken item do?
options: help with the repair
leave the item for a month
pay for any spare parts
book a place in advance
questions.explanation: Господар не йде: тримає ліхтар, подає деталі й по змозі робить останній крок.

questions.title: What does the text say about modern kettles and printers?
options: they are made not to open
they are cheaper to replace
they are repaired most often
they need special tools
questions.explanation: Чайники склеєні, а принтери ламаються від самого відкривання — їх свідомо так роблять.

questions.title: What do the organisers do with their list of failures?
options: they send it to manufacturers
they publish it in a newspaper
they give it to customers
they keep it for themselves
questions.explanation: Раз на рік перелік надсилають двом виробникам, які жодного разу не відповіли.

questions.title: What advice do the organisers give to people starting a café?
options: tools matter least
buy good equipment first
begin with bicycles only
work with a local school
questions.explanation: «Інструменти — найлегше. Рідкісний інструмент — терпіння».

questions.title: Why was the projector left in the building?
options: moving it cost too much
the owners hoped to return
it belonged to the town
it was too heavy to move
questions.explanation: Перевезти проєктор коштувало б більше, ніж він вартий.

questions.title: What were the three owners warned about?
options: the town was too small
the building was unsafe
the lease was too short
the projector was broken
questions.explanation: Казали, що поруч мультиплекс, у всіх підписки, а в місті менше дев’яти тисяч людей.

questions.title: How is the programme decided?
options: the audience votes for it
the owners choose it alone
a distributor supplies it
the school suggests it
questions.explanation: Два фільми на тиждень обирають голосуванням на дошці у фоє.

questions.title: Where does most of the cinema's money come from?
options: other uses of the hall
tickets sold at weekends
a grant from the town
the café in the foyer
questions.explanation: Квитки покривають близько половини витрат, решту дає оренда залу вдень.

questions.title: What does the owner mean by his last remark?
options: the room is what matters
the cinema will close again
the films are badly chosen
the chairs need replacing
questions.explanation: «Кімната з кріслами й темною стіною» — корисне саме приміщення, а не показ.

questions.title: Why did Marko start reading the rain gauge?
options: his grandmother asked him to
his school had set a project
the village needed the figures
he was interested in weather
questions.explanation: Бабуся подарувала дощомір і сказала знімати покази щоранку о восьмій.

questions.title: What does the writer say about the diary itself?
options: it makes for dull reading
it is hard to understand
it was written very neatly
it has gaps in the middle
questions.explanation: Читати його нецікаво: дата, число й зрідка одне слово.

questions.title: Why are the official figures of little use to the village?
options: they are measured elsewhere
they are published too late
they cover only the summer
they are kept by the council
questions.explanation: Найближчий офіційний дощомір за 26 км, за пасмом пагорбів, де опади зовсім інші.

questions.title: What did the village need the diary for?
options: to prove the floods grew
to plan the harvest better
to attract more visitors
to open a weather station
questions.explanation: Заявка на міст вимагала доказу, що підтоплення посилюються, — його дали записи Марка.

questions.title: How does Marko see the nine years of readings?
options: as a habit, not science
as a piece of real research
as time he wishes he had back
as a duty to his village
questions.explanation: «Це була не наука, а звичка. Наука вийшла випадково».

questions.title: How does the seed library work?
options: readers bring back more
readers pay a small deposit
seeds are lent for one season
seeds go to members only
questions.explanation: Принцип той самий, що й у книжок: візьми потрібне й поверни більше, ніж узяв.

questions.title: Why is returning seeds harder than returning books?
options: a plant must go to seed
the packets are easily lost
seeds go bad very quickly
few readers have a garden
questions.explanation: Насіння повернеться лише тоді, коли рослину не з’їдять, а дадуть визріти й висушать.

questions.title: How did the librarians react to the first year?
options: they taught seed saving
they charged for late returns
they bought seed from a shop
they closed the four drawers
questions.explanation: Замість докорів — чотири вечірні заняття, записка в кожному пакетику й вужчий вибір.

questions.title: Why were cucumbers and carrots withdrawn?
options: beginners fail with them
nobody ever asked for them
they take up too much room
their seeds are expensive
questions.explanation: Вони легко перезапилюються із сусідніми рослинами, тож у новачків майже не виходить.

questions.title: What is special about the yellow tomato?
options: no shop here sells it
it was bred by the library
it ripens earlier than others
it needs no watering at all
questions.explanation: У шухлядах є сорти, яких не продають у крамницях, — цей приніс хтось із Карпат.

questions.title: Why did the lighthouse stop working?
options: satellites replaced it
the last keeper retired
the building became unsafe
the spit was washed away
questions.explanation: Світло стало непотрібним 1998 року, коли з’явилася супутникова система.

questions.title: What was Oksana originally asked to do?
options: sell tickets at the door
write the history of the light
guide visitors round the tower
sort the keeper's logbooks
questions.explanation: Музей шукав волонтера, щоб продавати квитки на вихідних.

questions.title: Where did the letters she answered come from?
options: letters sent to the light
the museum in the nearby town
her friends in the village
the keeper who had left
questions.explanation: Листи й далі надходили на маяк: від любителів суден, школярів, моряка з Ґданська.

questions.title: What rule does Oksana insist on?
options: replies are handwritten
every visitor buys a ticket
the tower closes in winter
helpers must live nearby
questions.explanation: Жодних друкованих відповідей і жодного листа, що чекає понад два тижні.

questions.title: What does Oksana mean by calling a letter a lighthouse?
options: it stays with the reader
it warns people of danger
it is seen from far away
it costs almost nothing
questions.explanation: Корабель бачив світло мить, а лист приходить додому й лишається на столі.

questions.title: Match each message to what it is about.
pairs: Sorry, I'm still on the tram. There was an accident near the bridge and we've been standing for ten minutes. Start without me, I'll be there by half past.
arriving later than planned
Could you water the plants while we're away? The key is with Mrs Petrenko on the second floor. Twice a week is enough, and please don't feed the cat anything sweet.
a favour asked of a neighbour
Don't forget your passport this time. Check-in closes forty minutes before departure, so we should leave the house at five at the very latest.
a reminder before a journey
Your parcel is at the collection point on Hlibna Street until Thursday. Bring the code from this message and any document with your photograph.
picking something up
I read your essay on the train. The middle part is much stronger than last time, but the ending still stops too suddenly. Shall we go through it tomorrow?
an opinion on somebody's work
questions.explanation: Перше повідомлення пояснює запізнення, друге просить сусідську послугу, третє нагадує про документи перед дорогою, четверте — про видачу посилки, п’яте оцінює чужий текст. Запрошення, скарги чи пропозиції підвезти тут немає.

questions.title: Match each sign to what it tells you.
pairs: Wet paint. Please use the far staircase until Wednesday. We are sorry for the inconvenience.
not to touch something
Quiet zone. Phone calls and group work are not allowed beyond this point. Rooms for talking are on the ground floor.
how to behave in a room
Last entry 45 minutes before closing. The upper galleries are cleared fifteen minutes earlier than the rest.
when you may still come in
Lift out of service. Engineers are working on it today. Deliveries to the upper floors should be left at reception.
that something is not working
Tickets are valid for one journey in one direction. Validate yours as soon as you board, or a fine may be charged.
what you must do with a ticket
questions.explanation: Табличка про фарбу просить нічого не чіпати, друга описує правила поведінки, третя — час останнього входу, четверта повідомляє про несправність, п’ята — що робити з квитком.

questions.title: Match each announcement to what it is about.
pairs: From September, the school day will begin at 8:30 instead of 8:00. The last lesson will end twenty minutes later than it does now.
a change to a timetable
The chess club is looking for two more players for the regional tournament. Speak to Mr Levchenko in room 214 before the end of the week.
a search for new members
Photographs from the autumn trip are now on the noticeboard outside the staff room. Please write your name under any picture you would like a copy of.
how to get something you want
Because of the storm warning, tomorrow's sports day has been moved to the twenty-third. Everything else in the programme stays the same.
an event that has been put off
The canteen will accept cards from Monday. Cash will still be taken, but only at the window nearest the door.
a new way of paying
questions.explanation: Перше оголошення змінює розклад, друге шукає гравців, третє пояснює, як отримати копію світлини, четверте переносить свято, п’яте вводить оплату карткою.

questions.title: Match each short review to what the writer says.
pairs: The food was excellent and the prices fair, but we waited fifty minutes for a table we had booked two weeks earlier. Book, then bring your patience.
the service was slow
I bought this jacket for winter walking and it has survived two seasons of rain without letting in a drop. It is heavier than it looks, though.
the thing has lasted well
Beautiful views, friendly staff, and a bed that could have been made of stone. I slept badly for three nights and left with a sore back.
sleeping there was uncomfortable
The museum itself is small, but the guide made two hours pass like twenty minutes. Ask for Iryna if she is working that day.
one person made the visit
Cheap, quick and exactly what the photographs promised. There is nothing memorable about the place, and for one night that is a compliment.
it was good enough for the purpose
extraChoices: the price was far too high
the place was hard to find
questions.explanation: Перший відгук нарікає на очікування, другий хвалить довговічність, третій — про незручне ліжко, четвертий — про екскурсовода, п’ятий каже, що місце цілком годиться на одну ніч.

questions.title: Match each leaflet to what it offers.
pairs: Free hearing tests every Tuesday and Thursday morning. No appointment needed; simply bring a document with your date of birth.
a check on your health
We collect old phones, cables and batteries and take them apart safely. Drop your box at any of our four points; nothing is charged.
a way to get rid of waste
Saturday mornings in the yard behind the church: bring what you no longer wear, take what fits. Everything left at noon goes to the shelter.
an exchange of clothes
Our evening group meets on Wednesdays for anyone learning to read music as an adult. Instruments are provided for the first month.
lessons for grown-ups
Lost your keys? Our van comes to you, usually within the hour, and opens the door without damaging it. Day and night, all year.
help in an emergency
questions.explanation: Перша листівка пропонує безкоштовну перевірку слуху, друга — прийом електронного мотлоху, третя — обмін одягом, четверта — заняття для дорослих, п’ята — виклик майстра у скруті.

questions.title: Match each email to its purpose.
pairs: Thank you for your application. We have received more than four hundred this year and will write to everyone by 30 April, whatever the outcome.
to say an answer will come later
Your subscription ends on 12 May. If you do nothing, it will renew for another year at the same price as last time.
to warn that money will be taken
I attach the corrected version. Two dates in the second paragraph were wrong, and I have marked one sentence I could not understand at all.
to send back a corrected file
We are sorry that the lamp arrived broken. Keep the box, and our courier will collect it on Friday between nine and one.
to arrange a collection
Could everyone confirm by Thursday whether they are coming? The restaurant needs a number, and I would rather not guess.
to ask people to reply
questions.explanation: Перший лист обіцяє відповідь пізніше, другий попереджає про автоматичне продовження, третій повертає виправлений файл, четвертий домовляється про забір товару, п’ятий просить підтвердити участь.

questions.title: Match each poster to what it invites you to do.
pairs: Bring your bicycle to the square on Sunday and our mechanics will check the brakes and gears for free. Repairs beyond that are at normal prices.
have something looked at
Readers of all ages are welcome to sit with our volunteers and practise reading aloud for twenty minutes. No registration, no charge, no marks.
practise a skill with somebody
Sing with us on Thursday evenings. You do not need to read music, but you do need to come regularly, because we are preparing a concert.
join a group that meets often
Photographs of the old port wanted for next year's exhibition. Anything taken before 1995 is of interest; we scan and return everything the same day.
share something you own
Walk the river path with a biologist and learn to recognise the twelve commonest birds along it. Boots are essential; binoculars are lent.
learn about nature outdoors
questions.explanation: Перший плакат запрошує на безкоштовну перевірку велосипеда, другий — почитати вголос із волонтером, третій — до хору, четвертий просить поділитися старими світлинами, п’ятий кличе на прогулянку з біологом.

questions.title: Match each note left in a shared flat to what it is about.
pairs: Whoever used the last of the coffee: the shop on the corner opens at seven. I am not making any accusations. I am simply stating the facts.
something that has run out
The washing machine makes a loud noise on the fast spin. I have written to the landlord twice; if he ignores me again I will call somebody myself.
a repair nobody has done
My parents are staying on Friday and Saturday. They are quiet, they go to bed at nine, and they are bringing an enormous cake.
visitors who are coming
Please write down what you take from the shelf and we will settle up at the end of the month. Last time nobody remembered anything.
keeping track of money
The bin men now come on Tuesday, not Thursday. If the bags are not out by seven in the morning they are left for another week.
a new day for something
questions.explanation: Перша записка про каву, якої не лишилося, друга — про невиконаний ремонт, третя попереджає про гостей, четверта заводить облік витрат, п’ята повідомляє про новий день вивезення сміття.

questions.title: Match each classified advertisement to what is being offered.
pairs: Piano, upright, in tune, free to anyone who can carry it down two flights of stairs. It has been in the family since 1961 and deserves a home.
something given away
Experienced tailor takes in jackets, shortens trousers and repairs zips. Two days for most jobs, same day if you ask nicely and bring chocolate.
a service that mends clothes
Two rooms above the bakery, furnished, from October. Suitable for students; the rent includes heating but not electricity.
somewhere to live
Maths and physics, Years 7 to 11, at your home or mine. First lesson costs nothing so that we can both decide whether it is working.
help with school subjects
Small grey dog, answers to Tosha, last seen near the market on Saturday evening. He is friendly but will not come to strangers without food.
an animal that has gone missing
extraChoices: a holiday flat by the sea
questions.explanation: Перше оголошення віддає піаніно задарма, друге пропонує послуги кравця, третє здає кімнати, четверте — репетиторство, п’яте шукає загубленого собаку.

questions.title: Match each extract from a school website to what it explains.
pairs: Pupils who arrive after the second bell should go to the office, not straight to the classroom, so that the register can be corrected.
what to do if you are late
Mobile phones are collected in a box at the start of every lesson and returned at the end of it. Parents may always reach the office by telephone.
a rule about equipment
Anyone absent for more than three days needs a note from a doctor before returning. Without it, the absence is recorded as unexplained.
what you must bring after an illness
The library stays open until six on Tuesdays and Thursdays for anyone who prefers to work here rather than at home. A teacher is always present.
when a room is open in the evening
Lunch is ordered the day before on the tablet by the canteen door. Anyone who forgets is given soup, which is nobody's first choice.
how meals are arranged
extraChoices: how to apply to the school
how much a trip will cost
questions.explanation: Перший уривок пояснює, що робити після дзвінка, другий — правило про телефони, третій — довідку після хвороби, четвертий — вечірні години бібліотеки, п’ятий — як замовляють обід.

questions.title: Match each city museum to what it offers.
pairs: The Water Museum. Built inside a working pumping station, this museum explains where the city's water comes from and where it goes afterwards. Visitors walk along a glass floor above the pipes, and the guides are engineers who still work on the system.
is housed in a building that still works

The Museum of the Printed Word. Its collection covers five centuries of printing, but the room everyone remembers is the workshop, where visitors set a line of type by hand and take away the page they have printed.
lets visitors make something to keep

The Toy Archive. Nothing here is behind glass. The archive lends its collection of wooden and mechanical toys to hospitals and children's homes, and the rooms open to the public hold whatever happens to be back that week.
shows a collection that keeps changing
The House on Zelena Street. A merchant's house kept exactly as it was in 1908, down to the tea in the cupboard. Only eight people are admitted at a time, and shoes are left at the door.
admits very small groups only
The Museum of Everyday Sound. Recordings of trams, markets, factories and kitchens made between 1960 and today. Visitors sit in the dark with headphones; there is almost nothing to look at.
asks you to listen rather than look
The Salt Gallery. The oldest part of the mine was closed in 1974 and reopened as a gallery in 2005. The temperature never changes, which is why the paintings hanging there need no equipment at all.
keeps its exhibits without machinery
extraChoices: is free for visitors under sixteen
is open only in the summer months
questions.explanation: Музей води працює всередині діючої станції; друкарня дає забрати власноруч надруковану сторінку; архів іграшок постійно змінює експозицію, бо роздає її; будинок на Зеленій пускає по вісім осіб; музей звуку просить слухати; соляна галерея тримає картини без обладнання.

questions.title: Match each evening course to what it promises.
pairs: Bread from Scratch. Six Tuesdays, one loaf a week, starting with the simplest dough and ending with sourdough that takes three days. Everyone goes home with their bread, however it turns out.
builds up from easy to difficult
Speak in Public. A small group meets for eight weeks and every member speaks at every meeting, on a subject drawn out of a hat. The tutor films each talk and nobody else sees the recording.
gives feedback in private
Fixing Your Own Bicycle. Bring the bicycle you actually ride. By the end of four evenings you will have taken off both wheels, mended a puncture and adjusted your own brakes.
works on your own equipment
Reading Old Handwriting. For anybody trying to read family letters or parish records from the last two centuries. Slow, unglamorous and, according to former students, strangely addictive.
helps with documents from the past

Drawing on Saturdays. No talent required and none expected. The course is built on the idea that drawing is a way of looking, and half of every session is spent looking at things rather than at paper.
treats a skill as a way of seeing
Cooking for One. Designed for people who live alone and have stopped bothering. Recipes use one pan, cost little and make exactly one portion, which is the whole point.
suits people who cook for themselves
questions.explanation: Курс хліба веде від простого до складного; ораторський знімає виступи лише для самого учня; велосипедний працює з твоїм власним велосипедом; курс старого письма — про давні документи; малювання вчить дивитися; кулінарія — для тих, хто готує на одного.

questions.title: Match each walking route to what it is like.
pairs: The Aqueduct Path. Eleven kilometres along a nineteenth-century water channel, almost perfectly flat, with a handrail on the steep side. Wheelchairs and prams manage it easily in dry weather.
can be walked without climbing
The Three Chapels. A twenty-kilometre loop that connects three village chapels, each open and each with a stamp for walkers to collect. Most people take the whole day and eat at the second one.
rewards walkers who collect something
The Night Ridge. Best walked between midnight and dawn in June, when the path is easy to follow and the valley below fills with mist. A head torch is essential and the last stretch is steep.
is meant to be done in the dark
The Old Border. Six kilometres of forest track marked by stones cut in 1867. Information boards explain what the border separated and why it was moved, and a museum at the end fills in the rest.
explains the history of the place
The Quarry Circuit. A short route of four kilometres with no shade whatever. Start early, carry water, and do not attempt it between eleven and four in July or August.
should be avoided in the heat
The Ferry and Back. Walk out along one bank, cross on the small ferry, and return on the other side. The ferry runs hourly until six, and missing the last one means a long walk home.
depends on a timetable
extraChoices: charges a fee at the entrance
questions.explanation: Акведук рівний і доступний; маршрут трьох каплиць дає збирати печатки; нічний хребет ходять затемна; старий кордон розповідає історію; кар’єрне коло не для спеки; поромний залежить від розкладу.

questions.title: Match each student club to what it does.
pairs: The Debating Society. Members argue for whichever side they are given, not the one they believe in, and a coin decides. Meetings are on Mondays and the room is always too small.
asks members to defend any side
The Quiet Hour. Forty minutes of reading and twenty minutes of tea, every Wednesday, with no discussion of what anybody has read unless they want it. Attendance has trebled since it started.
leaves talking to those who wish to
The Repair Squad. Members mend furniture and equipment around the college, from wobbling chairs to the cupboard doors in the chemistry lab. The college supplies materials; the labour is free.
keeps its own building in order
The Recording Club. Students record interviews with people over seventy in their home towns and deposit the files with the regional archive. Fifty-four interviews have been collected so far.
preserves what older people remember
The Night Sky Group. Meets only when the forecast promises a clear sky, which means an announcement at four in the afternoon and a scramble for the minibus at nine.
meets when conditions allow
The Translation Circle. Members bring a page of anything they like — a poem, a manual, a menu — and the group argues over how to carry it into another language. Nothing is ever finished.
works on short pieces of text
questions.explanation: Дискусійний клуб змушує захищати будь-яку сторону; «Тиха година» лишає розмови охочим; ремонтна бригада лагодить власний корпус; клуб записів зберігає спогади старших; астрономи збираються за погодою; перекладацьке коло працює з короткими текстами.

questions.title: Match each hostel to what it is known for.
pairs: The Signal Box. Four rooms in a converted railway building beside a working line. Trains pass twice an hour until eleven at night, and the owners say so clearly before anyone books.
warns guests about the noise
Mill House. Guests are asked to leave their car at the gate and walk the last two hundred metres. There is no reception, only a board with names and room numbers written in chalk.
is run without any staff on duty
The Long Table. Breakfast is served at eight for everybody at once, at one table, and latecomers get what is left. Nobody has ever complained twice, because the food is very good.
makes guests eat together
Harbour Steps. Every room looks at the sea, and every room is reached by an outside staircase that is slippery in rain. Not suitable for anybody carrying much luggage.
is awkward to reach with bags
The Green Door. The cheapest beds in town, paid for by the café downstairs. Guests who work two hours a day in the café pay nothing at all, and most stay a fortnight.
lets guests pay with their work
Birch Yard. Twelve beds, open from May to September only, in a garden with an outdoor kitchen. The owners close it every winter and spend those months repairing what the summer broke.
opens for one season a year
extraChoices: includes all meals in the price
questions.explanation: «Сигнальна будка» чесно попереджає про потяги; Mill House працює без персоналу; The Long Table садить усіх за один стіл; Harbour Steps незручні з багажем; The Green Door дозволяє відпрацювати проживання; Birch Yard відкритий лише влітку.

questions.title: Match each mobile application to what it does.
pairs: Tidemark. Shows the height of the water at four hundred coastal points and warns you an hour before the path you are standing on is cut off. Works without a signal once the day is downloaded.
keeps working with no connection
Sorted. Photograph anything you are about to throw away and the application tells you which bin it belongs in, in your own town, with the local rules rather than the general ones.
answers a question about your own area
Nine Words. Sends you nine words of a language every morning and asks for them again three days later, then nine days later, then a month later. Nothing else, ever.
returns to material after a delay
Pantry. You list what is in the cupboard and it suggests what can be made from it tonight. The more honestly you list, the worse and more useful the suggestions become.
works from what you already have
Footfall. Counts how far you have walked and converts it into places: after eleven kilometres you have crossed a named bridge, after forty you have reached a named town.
turns your effort into a journey
Quiet Hours. Learns which of your applications you open after midnight and makes those, and only those, harder to reach. It cannot be switched off before morning.
makes some choices deliberately difficult
extraChoices: costs nothing for the first month
questions.explanation: Tidemark працює без мережі; Sorted відповідає за правилами конкретного міста; Nine Words повертає слова через паузи; Pantry виходить із наявних продуктів; Footfall перетворює кілометри на подорож; Quiet Hours навмисно ускладнює доступ.

questions.title: Match each festival to what makes it unusual.
pairs: The Harvest Table. One street, one table six hundred metres long, and every household brings a dish. Visitors pay nothing but are expected to bring something too, however small.
expects guests to contribute food
Lantern Week. For seven evenings the street lamps in the old town are switched off and the only light comes from paper lanterns hung by residents. Shops stay open and torches are frowned upon.
turns off the usual lighting
The Short Film Night. Forty films, none longer than four minutes, shown on the wall of a grain store. The audience votes by moving from one side of the yard to the other.
asks the audience to decide
Sheep Sunday. Once a year the flocks are driven through the middle of town to their summer pasture, and the main street closes for three hours. Nobody organised the first one.
grew out of ordinary work
The Silent Disco by the River. Three hundred people dance on the embankment wearing headphones, so the loudest sound is footsteps. Neighbours who once objected now sell tea.
makes almost no noise
The Repair Fair. Bring one broken thing and one skill. Everybody who mends something for a stranger has something of their own mended in return, and no money changes hands.
runs on an exchange of help
extraChoices: is held indoors when it rains
questions.explanation: На «Столі врожаю» гості теж щось приносять; Lantern Week гасить ліхтарі; на ночі коротких фільмів голосує глядач; «Овеча неділя» виросла зі звичайного перегону отари; тиха дискотека майже беззвучна; ремонтний ярмарок будується на обміні послугами.

questions.title: Match each volunteer project to what volunteers do.
pairs: River Watch. Volunteers take a sample of water from the same point every fortnight, test it with a kit and enter three numbers online. Ten minutes a time, for years on end.
repeat a small task over a long time
Read Aloud. Pairs of volunteers visit hospital wards in the afternoons and read to patients who cannot hold a book. They are asked never to choose the book themselves.
let other people make the choice
The Lost Names. Volunteers photograph gravestones in village cemeteries before the lettering disappears and type what they can still read into a shared list.
record something before it is gone
Warm Line. Volunteers telephone older people who live alone, at a time the person chooses, and talk about nothing in particular for twenty minutes a week.
give company by telephone
Bicycle Bank. Volunteers collect abandoned bicycles, mend them over the winter and give them in spring to people who need transport to work. Six hundred have been handed over so far.
repair things and pass them on
Night Count. One night in February, volunteers walk a fixed route in pairs and count how many people are sleeping outside. The figure decides how much money the city receives.
gather numbers that affect funding
questions.explanation: River Watch — те саме коротке вимірювання роками; Read Aloud лишає вибір книжки пацієнтові; The Lost Names фіксує написи, поки вони є; Warm Line дає товариство телефоном; Bicycle Bank лагодить і віддає; Night Count збирає цифри, від яких залежить фінансування.

questions.title: Match each bookshop to what it is like.
pairs: Page and Post. Half bookshop, half post office, because the village could not keep either on its own. Parcels are weighed on the counter between the poetry and the maps.
shares its room with another service
The Second Shelf. Nothing on sale is new, and nothing costs more than the price written in pencil by whoever donated it. The money goes to the school next door.
sells only what people have given
Cover Story. Every book in the window is wrapped in brown paper with three lines about it and no title. You choose blind, and you may bring it back if you have read it before.
hides what the books are called
The Reading Room. Customers may sit and read all day without buying anything, and many do. The owner says the coffee pays for the chairs and the chairs pay for the books.
allows reading without buying
Lighthouse Books. Open from Thursday to Sunday, because the owner teaches for the rest of the week. The hours are on the door and have never once changed.
opens on only a few days
The Corner Stock. Fewer than three hundred titles, each chosen by a staff member who writes a card explaining why. When a title sells out it is replaced by a different one.
keeps a small, personal selection
extraChoices: orders any book within a day
is the oldest shop in the town
questions.explanation: Page and Post ділить приміщення з поштою; The Second Shelf продає лише подароване; Cover Story ховає назви; The Reading Room дозволяє читати без покупки; Lighthouse Books відчинена кілька днів на тиждень; The Corner Stock тримає малий особистий добір.

questions.title: Match each school trip to what pupils gain from it.
pairs: Three days at a working dairy farm. Pupils get up at five with the farmer, and the timetable is the animals' rather than the school's. Most say the hardest part is the hour before breakfast.
learn to follow somebody else's routine
A morning at the regional court, watching real hearings from the public seats. A judge answers questions afterwards, and pupils are warned that they may hear unpleasant details.
see how a profession really works
A week in a town where nobody speaks their language. Pupils stay with families, and teachers deliberately answer questions in the other language only.
manage without their own language
A day of measuring a stream: depth, speed, temperature and what lives in it. The results are added to a ten-year record that the school keeps with a university.
add to work that others continue
Two nights in a mountain hut with no electricity and no shop. Everything eaten has to be carried up, and everything left over has to be carried down again.
carry what they need with them
An afternoon in the archive, where each pupil is given one document from their own street and asked to find out what happened on it. Nobody is told the answer.
work something out for themselves
questions.explanation: Ферма вчить жити за чужим розкладом; суд показує справжню професію; тиждень без рідної мови змушує давати раду інакше; вимірювання струмка додає дані до довгого ряду; гірська хатина — усе несеш на собі; архів лишає учня з документом сам на сам.

questions.title: Match each radio programme to what it is about.
pairs: Twelve Minutes. One guest, one object they have kept for more than twenty years, and the story of why it is still in the house. There is no music and no second question.
one thing that somebody has kept
The Wrong Answer. Scientists describe an experiment that failed and what they understood afterwards. The presenter says it is the only programme where nobody is allowed to sound certain.
mistakes that led somewhere
Night Buses. Recorded between one and four in the morning on city routes, with drivers and passengers who agree to talk. Very little is edited out.
conversations at unusual hours
Small Print. Each week one contract that ordinary people sign — a phone, a flat, a gym — read slowly, line by line, with a lawyer explaining the parts nobody reads.
documents people sign without reading
Second Language. Adults who moved country after forty describe the first year of speaking badly. Listeners send in the sentence that embarrassed them most.
learning to speak as an adult
The Quiet Map. Recordings from the twenty quietest places the producers can find, broadcast without commentary for half an hour on Sunday mornings.
sound with nobody talking over it
questions.explanation: «Дванадцять хвилин» — про одну збережену річ; The Wrong Answer — про невдалі досліди; Night Buses — розмови вночі; Small Print розбирає договори; Second Language — про дорослих, що вчать мову; The Quiet Map дає звук без коментаря.
